title: Discord Join Call
blurb: The Discord join sound — that friendly little blip announcing someone just entered the call. It's Pavlovian at this point: a generation of gamers hears it and instinctively says a name as a question. Use it in edits to signal an arrival, or play it in a real call to convince everyone a ghost member just joined. Simple, iconic, endlessly abusable.
origin: Discord's default voice-channel join notification.

title: Discord Leave Call
blurb: The Discord leave sound — the descending blip of someone dipping from the call. Sometimes it means goodnight; sometimes it means they lost the argument and rage-quit, and the sound plays exactly the same either way, which is the beauty of it. Play it after any conversational L to imply the loser has left the building. A perfect passive-aggressive punctuation mark.
origin: Discord's default voice-channel disconnect notification.

title: Discord Notification
blurb: The Discord message notification — the soft double-knock that means someone needs you, or more likely, someone posted a meme at 2am. Like all great notification sounds it triggers an involuntary phone-check in anyone who's ever used the app. Essential for edits about gamers, group chats, and being perceived. Also elite prank material in any room full of Discord users.
origin: Discord's default incoming-message sound.

title: Discord Ping
blurb: The Discord ping — the sharper alert of being @mentioned, which is to say: summoned. There is no peace once this sound plays; somebody wants something and they want it publicly. Use it in edits when a character gets called out by name, or to dramatize the horror of '@everyone'. The sound of your name being spoken in a server you forgot you joined.
origin: Discord's mention/ping alert sound.

title: And His Name Is John Cena
blurb: AND HIS NAME IS JOHN CENA — the trumpet fanfare plus that legendary announcement, meme-ified into the universal sound of a surprise entrance. It plays when anyone or anything arrives unexpectedly and with maximum force: the pizza guy, the plot twist, your mom when the lights were supposed to be off. One of the defining prank sounds of an entire internet era.
origin: John Cena's WWE entrance announcement, immortalized by the unexpected-Cena prank meme.

title: The Rock Eyebrow
blurb: The Rock's eyebrow-raise sound — the dramatic sting attached to the most famous skeptical face on the internet. When someone says something questionable, the eyebrow goes up and this sound plays; those are simply the rules now. Use it for doubtful pauses, side-eyes, and any statement that requires silent, muscular scrutiny before a response.
origin: The sting paired with Dwayne Johnson's iconic raised-eyebrow reaction meme.

title: Erm, What the Sigma?
blurb: Erm, what the sigma? — the brainrot-era catchphrase that fuses ironic sigma-male culture with pure Gen Alpha chaos. It's the designated response to anything mildly unusual, delivered in a tone of scandalized confusion. Whether you use it sincerely or as anthropological commentary on the youth, it lands. A time capsule of the skibidi era, preserved in button form.
origin: A brainrot catchphrase from the skibidi/sigma meme era.

title: Nothing Beats a Jet2 Holiday
blurb: Nothing beats a Jet2 holiday — the relentlessly cheerful British airline ad audio that TikTok turned into the soundtrack of chaos. The joke: play the sunny jingle and voiceover over footage of things going catastrophically wrong on actual holidays. The bigger the disaster, the harder the chipper delivery hits. One of the biggest audio memes of recent years, especially in the UK.
origin: From Jet2's TV advert; viral on TikTok as ironic backing for holiday disasters.

title: Sad Hamster
blurb: The Sad Hamster sound — the mournful violin paired with that wide-eyed hamster staring into your soul. It became the internet's mascot for being small, pitiful, and dramatically wronged: use it when your order arrives wrong, when the meeting could have been an email, when it starts raining the second you leave. Peak cuteness deployed as peak melodrama.
origin: The viral wide-eyed hamster meme with sad violin backing (from the 'Hampter' family of memes).

title: Banana Cat Crying
blurb: The crying Banana Cat — a cat in a banana costume sobbing its heart out, and somehow one of the most emotionally resonant sounds on the internet. It's the audio for cute-sad situations: minor injustices, wholesome disappointments, watching your food get eaten by someone else. The genre is 'devastating but adorable' and this is its national anthem.
origin: From the Banana Cat meme videos — a costumed cat crying dramatically.

title: Goku Drip
blurb: The Goku Drip sound — the beat that plays whenever someone's outfit goes impossibly hard, canonized by the legendary image of Goku in Supreme. 'Drip' culture and anime collided and this audio was the result. Use it for fit checks, glow-ups, and anyone stepping out with unearned confidence. The drip is non-negotiable; the sound makes it official.
origin: From the viral 'Drip Goku' meme — Goku in streetwear, awarded maximum drip.

title: Nuh Uh
blurb: Nuh uh — the childlike, utterly unbothered denial that ends any argument by simply refusing to engage with it. No counter-evidence, no logic, just: nuh uh. TikTok made it the official response to accusations, facts, and consequences alike. It is legally impossible to argue with. The most efficient defensive tool in the meme arsenal.
origin: A viral childlike denial clip; the internet's official rebuttal to everything.

title: Yippee (TBH Creature)
blurb: The Yippee sound — a squeaky little celebration noise attached to the beloved TBH Creature. It's pure, small, sincere joy: use it for tiny wins, good news, free food, and any moment that deserves a modest party. The internet has plenty of ironic sounds; this one is genuinely happy, which makes it weirdly precious. Yippee!
origin: The celebration squeak paired with the TBH Creature meme.

title: You're Not That Guy, Pal
blurb: 'You're not that guy, pal. Trust me, you're not that guy.' — the calm, devastating reality check that became the internet's favorite way to deflate tough-guy energy. It's not shouted; that's what makes it lethal. Play it when someone's confidence writes a check their abilities can't cash: gym clips, ranked lobbies, corporate LinkedIn posts. Instant humility delivery system.
origin: From a viral street-interview clip; the definitive tough-guy deflation line.

title: Nut Button
blurb: The Nut Button sound — the slam of the big blue button labeled NUT, the meme format for irresistible urges of every kind. The joke long ago generalized past its origin: now the button gets slammed for any temptation immediately surrendered to — snoozing alarms, buying the thing, eating the last slice. Play the slam when resistance was never really on the table.
origin: From the blue 'nut button' image meme, generalized to any instantly-surrendered urge.

title: Clown Horn
blurb: The clown horn honk — the official soundtrack of foolishness. Meme culture assigns this sound to anyone mid-clownery: bad decisions in progress, confident wrong answers, people arguing with obvious bait. The double honk carries centuries of circus heritage straight into the group chat. Pairs perfectly with the full clown-makeup application meme. Honk honk.
origin: The classic circus bulb horn, meme shorthand for clown behavior.

title: Price Is Right Losing Horn
blurb: The Price Is Right losing horn — the four descending womp-womp notes of televised defeat. Decades of game-show failure trained everyone to feel this sound in their chest. It's the polished, network-TV cousin of the sad trombone: play it when a plan fails publicly and with witnesses. The definitive fanfare for losing gracefully on camera.
origin: The losing horn from The Price Is Right game show.

title: It Was at This Moment He Knew
blurb: 'It was at this moment that he knew… he f'd up.' The deadpan narrator line that plays in the frozen second between mistake and consequence. A cornerstone of fail-video editing: the skateboard mid-air, the firework tilting, the reply-all sent. The narration transforms disaster into documentary. One of the most quoted editing sounds of all time.
origin: The narrator line from classic fail-video edits of the mid-2010s.

title: Bombastic Side Eye
blurb: Bombastic side eye. Criminal offensive side eye. The viral audio that gave judgmental looks their own theme song. Play it over any glance that contains a full paragraph of disapproval: pets watching you eat their treats, coworkers hearing your excuse, grandmas evaluating your life choices. The sound does the judging so the eyes don't have to work alone.
origin: A viral TikTok audio pairing dramatic vocals with judgmental looks.

title: GYATT
blurb: GYATT — the scandalized exclamation that escaped streamer culture and conquered the brainrot lexicon. Officially it expresses astonishment; unofficially it's one of the load-bearing words of Gen Alpha vocabulary and using it out loud instantly reveals how online you are. Deploy the button ironically, anthropologically, or at your own reputational risk.
origin: From streamer slang, absorbed into the Gen Alpha brainrot canon.

title: Michael Jackson Hee-Hee
blurb: The Michael Jackson hee-hee — the most famous vocal ad-lib in pop history, meme-ified as an all-purpose exclamation of flair. It punctuates smooth moves, dramatic exits, and moments of unearned confidence. Anything done with a little extra style earns the hee-hee, and the button delivers it on demand. Undefeated since 1987.
origin: Michael Jackson's signature vocal ad-lib, meme shorthand for doing anything with flair.

title: What Da Dog Doin?
blurb: 'What da dog doin?' — the profound philosophical question posed whenever a dog is doing absolutely anything. The clip's genius is its universal applicability: the dog is always doin something, and the question always deserves asking. Play it over any animal mid-activity, or any human behaving inexplicably. One of the purest, dumbest, most beloved sounds online.
origin: From a viral video of someone earnestly asking what the dog is doing.

title: Doge Bonk
blurb: BONK — the cartoon thwack of the Doge bonk meme, where a bat-wielding Cheems delivers instant correction to bad thoughts. It's the internet's disciplinary instrument: play it when someone posts something cursed, says something unhinged, or needs immediate redirection to horny jail. The sound is the punishment and the punchline in one swing.
origin: From the Doge/Cheems 'bonk' meme — the corrective bat of the internet.

title: Pufferfish Eating Carrot
blurb: The pufferfish eating a carrot — the crunch heard around the world. This clip of a pufferfish demolishing a carrot became an inexplicably legendary meme sound: the crunch is violent, rhythmic, and hypnotic. Use it for eating scenes, destruction montages, or as a jumpscare for anyone with misophonia. Nobody knows why it's this funny. It just is.
origin: From the viral video of a pufferfish loudly eating a carrot.

title: Tuna
blurb: The Tuna sound — the clip that launched a thousand searches for 'tuna soundboard.' It's an absurdist little audio whose entire appeal is how confidently it says what it says. Use it as a non-sequitur interrupt, a conversation reset, or proof that the internet will make anything famous. If you know, you know; if you don't, press the button.
origin: The viral 'tuna' clip popularized through soundboard culture.

title: My Leg!
blurb: MY LEG! — Fred the Fish's anguished cry, SpongeBob's longest-running background gag. Any Bikini Bottom catastrophe, no matter how contained, somehow injures this one man's leg. The meme usage honors the original: play it for collateral damage, minor injuries treated as tragedies, and any group activity that claims an innocent bystander. A hall-of-fame running joke.
origin: Fred the Fish's recurring injury cry from SpongeBob SquarePants.

title: One Eternity Later
blurb: 'One eternity later…' — the SpongeBob time card for waits that transcend mortal patience. Where 'a few moments later' covers ordinary delays, this one is for the DMV, the group project partner's reply, and the friend who said they're five minutes away. The French narrator's weary delivery implies even he aged during the wait. Essential transition material.
origin: The exaggerated time card from SpongeBob SquarePants.

title: SpongeBob Fail
blurb: The SpongeBob fail sting — the show's dedicated sound for plans collapsing in real time. Bikini Bottom's writers understood failure comedy at a molecular level, and this sting is the proof: it lands with just enough drama to make small disasters feel ceremonial. Use it when the attempt was sincere and the result was not. A gentler, sillier cousin of the sad trombone.
origin: A failure sting from SpongeBob SquarePants' legendary sound design.

title: I'm SpongeBob!
blurb: 'I'm SpongeBob!' — the sponge introducing himself with the unearned confidence of a man who has never once read a room. It's a perfect entrance sound: play it when arriving anywhere, volunteering for anything, or claiming an identity nobody questioned. The sheer enthusiasm is the joke, and it never runs out. Who lives in a pineapple indeed.
origin: SpongeBob's enthusiastic self-introduction from the series.

title: Ah Sh*t, Here We Go Again
blurb: 'Ah sh*t, here we go again.' — CJ's weary opening line from GTA San Andreas, reborn as the universal sigh of recurring problems. Monday mornings, family group chat drama, the printer being out of ink again: all of it is Grove Street business now. One of gaming's most quoted lines, perfectly calibrated for life's reruns.
origin: CJ's iconic line from Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas' opening mission.

title: The Bomb Has Been Planted
blurb: 'The bomb has been planted.' — the Counter-Strike announcer line that instantly raises every heart rate in the server. Twenty-five years of clutch rounds live inside this sentence. The meme usage applies it to any point of no return: the message sent, the oven left on, the decision made. From here, everything is consequences. Iconic in esports and beyond.
origin: The bomb-plant announcement from Counter-Strike.

title: Enemy Spotted
blurb: 'Enemy spotted.' — the Counter-Strike radio callout, delivered with the flat professionalism of a man about to be one-tapped. It's gaming's most reusable alert: play it when the teacher walks in, when your ex enters the party, when the group chat's main character comes online. Threat detected, situational awareness engaged, good luck everyone.
origin: The classic radio callout from Counter-Strike.

title: Fire in the Hole (Geometry Dash)
blurb: FIRE IN THE HOLE — the Geometry Dash lobby clip that Gen Alpha turned into a certified brainrot anthem. The delivery is so unhinged that it stopped meaning anything about explosives and started meaning chaos itself. Play it before any reckless action: entering ranked, texting first, opening the family group chat. The hole is metaphorical; the fire is real.
origin: From Geometry Dash's lobby sounds, resurrected as a brainrot meme.

title: Minecraft Skeleton
blurb: The Minecraft skeleton rattle — the dry bone-clatter that means arrows are incoming and your dirt house is insufficient. For millions of players this sound triggers combat instincts calibrated in childhood. Use it for spooky-but-not-scary moments, skeleton war content, or ambushing a Minecraft player who thought they were safe. Doot-adjacent, danger-certified.
origin: The skeleton mob sound from Minecraft (Mojang).

title: Minecraft Damage (Oof)
blurb: The Minecraft damage sound — that blunt, dusty 'oof' of taking a hit, unchanged for over a decade and burned into gaming's collective memory. It works on anything: stubbed toes, roasts landing, fall damage both literal and emotional. Alongside the Roblox oof it forms the sacred duo of blocky-game pain sounds. Simple, iconic, eternally funny.
origin: The classic player-damage grunt from Minecraft.

title: Metal Gear Alert (!)
blurb: The Metal Gear Solid alert — that piercing '!' sting of a guard spotting Snake. It's the definitive being-noticed sound: play it when someone catches you mid-snack at 3am, when the boss walks past your screen, when eye contact happens at the worst moment. Stealth failed, alert phase initiated. One of gaming's most perfect two-note stories.
origin: The guard-alert '!' sting from Metal Gear Solid (Konami).

title: Mario Jump
blurb: The Mario jump — the springy boing that launched a billion platforming attempts. It's the most famous jump sound ever recorded, and applying it to real-world hops, leaps, and falls upgrades them all into gameplay. Use it for anything leaving the ground: cats, toddlers, stock prices before the crash. Forty years old and still full of air.
origin: The jump sound from Super Mario Bros. (Nintendo, 1985).

title: Fortnite Death Sound
blurb: The Fortnite death sound — the crunchy elimination thud that ended a hundred million matches. For an entire generation this is what defeat sounds like, which makes it perfect for real-world eliminations too: rejected texts, failed exams, getting picked last. Play it at the exact moment of elimination for maximum battle-royale realism.
origin: The player-elimination sound from Fortnite (Epic Games).

title: Nice Shot (Wii Sports)
blurb: 'Nice shot!' — the Wii Sports announcer's chipper approval, the most sincere compliment in gaming history. The Wii-era nostalgia is powerful, but the meme value is in ironic deployment: play it for terrible decisions executed confidently, parallel parking attempts, and any 'shot' that absolutely was not nice. The announcer believes in you even when he shouldn't.
origin: The announcer compliment from Wii Sports (Nintendo, 2006).

title: Get Griddy
blurb: The Griddy music — the beat behind Fortnite's most famous dance emote, escaped into real life. NFL end zones, school hallways, weddings: the Griddy conquered them all, and this audio is its engine. Play it whenever a celebration is about to happen, deserved or otherwise. The dance is optional but strongly implied by the button press.
origin: The music from Fortnite's Get Griddy emote, based on the viral dance.

title: Hitmarker
blurb: The hitmarker sound — the sharp tick of a Call of Duty shot connecting, cornerstone of the entire MLG montage genre. Every 360-noscope edit ever made runs on this sound stacked twelve deep. Use it for direct hits of any kind: comebacks landing, roasts connecting, dodgeballs finding their target. The crunchier the stack, the harder the play.
origin: The shot-confirmation tick from Call of Duty, core of MLG montage culture.

title: Ta-Da!
blurb: TA-DA! — the classic fanfare of a reveal, sincere or otherwise. The Windows-era jingle energy makes it perfect for both real accomplishments and absolute nothingburgers presented with showmanship: cleaning one dish, arriving on time, finishing the task that was due last week. The gap between fanfare and achievement is where the comedy lives.
origin: The classic reveal fanfare, in the tradition of the Windows 3.1 'tada' chime.

title: Drum Roll
blurb: The drum roll — professional-grade anticipation, on demand. Every announcement becomes an event when it rides in on a snare roll: raffle results, gender reveals, deciding where to eat. The longer you let it run, the higher the stakes climb, regardless of how little is actually at stake. Cut it with a cymbal or a fart; both are correct.
origin: The classic snare drum roll of announcements and reveals.

title: Sitcom Laugh Track
blurb: The sitcom laugh track — canned studio laughter that declares a joke has occurred, whether or not one did. That's the meme power: play it after anything and the anything becomes a punchline. Awkward silences, bad news delivered cheerfully, your own life choices — all improved by an invisible audience finding them hilarious. Comedy's oldest special effect after the fart.
origin: Classic canned studio-audience laughter from the sitcom era.

title: Crowd Cheering
blurb: A full crowd erupting in cheers — stadium-grade validation in one button. Play it for genuine victories or, better, for the tiniest possible accomplishments: getting out of bed, replying to the email, parallel parking on the first try. Everyone deserves an arena moment occasionally; this button democratizes the standing ovation.
origin: Stadium crowd cheering — the universal victory ambience.

title: Crickets (Awkward Silence)
blurb: Crickets — the sound of a joke landing in an empty field. When a punchline flops, a question goes unanswered, or the group chat reads the message and says nothing, the crickets speak for everyone. It's the most elegant way to certify a flop ever devised: nature itself declining to react. Deploy generously; someone always deserves it.
origin: The classic cricket chirp of comedic silence.

title: Eagle Screech
blurb: The eagle screech — the piercing cry that Hollywood attached to every bald eagle and America attached to everything else. It plays over flags, freedom, trucks, and fireworks; the meme usage adds grills, questionable patriotism, and anyone doing something aggressively American. Fun fact: real bald eagles sound much less impressive — this screech is usually a red-tailed hawk. The legend endures anyway.
origin: The iconic 'eagle' screech (usually a red-tailed hawk in reality), meme shorthand for America.

title: Undertaker Bell
blurb: The Undertaker's bell — the funeral toll that froze arenas for three decades. When the gong hits, someone's fate is sealed; that's true in WWE and truer in the group chat. Play it when a terrible decision is announced, when someone gets called into a meeting with HR, or when the '. ' text arrives. Doom, ceremonially delivered.
origin: The entrance gong of WWE's The Undertaker.

title: F1 Box Box
blurb: 'Box, box.' — the Formula 1 radio call to pit, delivered in that unmistakable compressed engineer voice. F1's boom turned it into shorthand for any strategic retreat: leaving the party, abandoning the argument, tactically exiting the family dinner. When conditions change, you box. Play the button and get in the pit lane of life.
origin: The pit-stop radio call from Formula 1 race engineering.

title: Netflix Tudum
blurb: TU-DUM — the Netflix intro sound, the two-note thud that starts a billion evenings. It signals that the next several hours are now spoken for. Use it in edits to announce that something dramatic is beginning, or play it in real life before any story time. One of the most successful pieces of sonic branding ever made, and everyone can sing it.
origin: Netflix's signature 'tudum' intro sting.

title: Love Island Text
blurb: 'I've got a text!' — the Love Island notification sound plus the scream that follows it. In the villa, this sound means drama is being delivered by SMS; on the internet, it means the same thing anywhere. Play it when any message arrives that's about to change everything: the results, the reply, the 'we need to talk.' A UK cultural institution in one button.
origin: The dramatic text-arrival sound from Love Island UK.

title: FaceTime Hang Up
blurb: The FaceTime hang-up sound — the blunt double-tap that ends the call. As a meme it's the sound of a conversation being terminated with prejudice: someone says something wild, and this plays. No goodbye, no explanation, just the void. The politest possible way to communicate 'absolutely not.' Devastating in edits, cathartic in real life.
origin: Apple's FaceTime call-end sound, memed as the ultimate conversation ender.

title: Ring Doorbell
blurb: The Ring doorbell chime — the modern doorbell sound that half the internet now recognizes from viral porch videos. It carries strange authority: someone is at the door and they are being recorded. Use it in edits to announce arrivals, or play it at home to make everyone freeze mid-sentence and check the app. Surveillance-era ding-dong.
origin: The chime from Ring video doorbells, famous via viral doorbell-cam footage.

title: School Bell
blurb: The school bell — the harsh ring that has governed childhood schedules for a century. It triggers deep instincts in everyone who's ever had a locker: the Pavlovian urge to stand up and leave, regardless of what's happening. Play it mid-meeting and watch grown adults reflexively start packing. Also perfect for edits about escapes, deadlines, and freedom.
origin: The classic school period bell.

title: Smoke Detector Beep
blurb: The smoke detector low-battery chirp — a single high beep, followed by silence, followed by madness. It's the most psychologically devastating sound in any home: impossible to locate, impossible to ignore, arriving exactly once every 43 seconds at 3am. As a prank it's a war crime. Play it near anyone and watch them lose their mind hunting a detector that doesn't exist.
origin: The universal low-battery chirp of smoke detectors everywhere.

title: Womp Womp
blurb: Womp womp — the verbal sad trombone, said directly to someone's face. TikTok revived it as the official response to complaints that will not be receiving sympathy: consequences of the person's own actions, minor inconveniences presented as tragedies, villains getting exactly what they ordered. Two syllables, zero sympathy, total conversation closure.
origin: The spoken 'womp womp' dismissal, revived as a viral TikTok response.

title: Oh Brother, This Guy Stinks!
blurb: 'Oh brother, this guy STINKS!' — the exasperated review that became the internet's favorite instant verdict. The delivery is pure New York jury duty energy: no appeal, no deliberation, the man simply stinks. Play it when anyone underperforms publicly — game lobbies, cooking attempts, karaoke. The people have spoken and the ruling is final.
origin: A viral reaction clip adopted as the internet's harshest instant review.

title: Yo Phone Linging
blurb: 'YO PHONE LINGING' — the deep-fried announcement that your phone is, indeed, ringing. The mispronunciation is the entire meme: it's your ringtone's chaotic evil form. Set it as an actual ringtone if you dare, play it when anyone's phone goes off in public, or use it to announce calls that absolutely should not be answered. Linging intensifies.
origin: A viral deep-fried 'your phone ringing' announcement clip.

title: Happy Happy Happy Cat
blurb: The Happy Happy Happy cat song — the chirpy tune attached to the world's most content little cat, and one of TikTok's most beloved wholesome audios. It's pure serotonin: play it for good news, small joys, pets doing anything at all. The internet runs on irony, but this sound is 100% sincere happiness and everyone has silently agreed to protect it.
origin: The viral 'happy happy happy' cat meme song from TikTok.
